title: Vibe coded entire think in a month. I feel like cheating.
author: ignas_HF
selftext:
So this is my first game coded entirely by AI. It is similar scale to my last game which took to reach same development point in 4.5 months(coded manually) and in this game reached same point in 1 month with AI.

The game is made in Unity and I was surprised to see that Codex can perfectly work with it. It also helped me with scriptable objects and making editor scripts which gave me deep control of game systems.  Also codex did balance of the game(will still need manual tweaks) but it saved me crazy amount of time.

So all scripts 100% vibecoded by Codex. For steam page I hired capsule artist(I think 700$ well spent)

Check Steam page for more - [GnomeBoozled](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4794780/GnomeBoozled/) 

I'm curious how people feel about this, hope game is still "AI enough" for you guys since 3D art is not AI made. For 3D made around 20% of stuff myself and rest is assets.

https://reddit.com/link/1ug9jrg/video/vrnrkhwd7n9h1/player

comments.author: Aineisa
comments.body:
I’m sure the early photographers felt they were “cheating.”

There’s nothing wrong with using a tool. 

I think we should be more concerned about how this changes the market. 

Are we going to see people make the games they want to play or will we still see game devs design and build something that can be sold?

I still think the latter because making something good still takes a lot of time and design skill (as demonstrated by a lot of the slop in this sub) 

But just recently I wanted to create a video with moving borders like those historical battle videos you find on YouTube. 

Not wanting to learn how to use DaVinci I just asked AI and it built such a good prototype specifically designed for such videos I now just use that. Neat but scary how I can cook exactly what I need at home

replies.author: ignas_HF
replies.body:
The market question is what's actually interesting to me. I think commercial devs will still chase what sells — but the long tail shifts. Solo devs with a weird specific vision who could never finish anything before might now actually ship. The cost of a weird bet goes down.

Your DaVinci thing is exactly that. You didn't want to learn a whole tool for one niche use case — you just wanted the thing. That used to mean it didn't get made.

replies.body: In a marketplace like this, the bottleneck becomes distribution. My strategy is to build a platform wide and fast. One hit feeds the next and hopefully we can beat the rising tide. Of games. Whatever.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
The market is totally fucking saturated with the latter.  Like 90% of the posts in these topics are by people just looking to churn slop for an income stream.  The asset flippers are out in force on this stuff.

The real test is when some of the passion projects start getting big enough to go to publishers with.  Will they care how much of it was "vibe coded" or will they care if you can continue to support and build the product after they fund art, sfx, marketing, voice acting, etc even if Claude is writing most of the line by line code.  It's a real risk sticking point, they'll need to be absolutely confident that you're not just yoloing it and the product isn't a dumpster fire under the hood that you can't handle when it breaks.

replies.author: Aineisa
replies.body:
I think you’re correct. Building an audience will become way more important than ever which unfortunately means devs have to do even more social media. 

Publishers will start to care more about audience size and past works. If you’ve demonstrated you’re creative and prolific with a large audience you’ll probably get picked up in a heartbeat.

replies.author: CuriousGio
replies.body:
In 2025, 1900 ganes were published on Steam, about 50 games PER DAY.

WHO has time to play them all?

Now that anybody can make a casual game, the winning game will depend on the Idea and the execution. Most people lack these two traits — the ability to generate good ideas, and having the taste to know the difference between good and bad.

Most people have had a friend who raves about a specific film or song that they absolutely love. They try to convince you it's the best song ever written. The you make the mistake of listening to it and you absolutely hate it. You wonder what type of person can think that's a good song.

The world is filled with people with bad taste so don't worry about the illusion that there's a lot of competition —AS LONG AS YOU HAVE TASTE. Don't be that person who thinks every idea you have is a brilliant idea. Figure out if you have good taste, or not.

Ultimately, taste and creativity are the two most critical skills from now until you die. Now that the technical part is taken care of by AI, the only thing that will lead to success is having good ideas that appeal to an audience, and having the taste to know what's good and bad.

Even if Ai isn't there yet in terms of being able to make any game one might imagine, just wait 6 months and we'll be there.

It would be wise to spend most of ones time on the concept and prototyping, coupled with market research. Most people skip the research part, like what type of games are people searching for every month. One can cater their concept to a specific market, such as people looking for science based games or math, or games for women, games you can play with friends, etc.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
>It would be wise to spend most of ones time on the concept and prototyping, coupled with market research. Most people skip the research part, like what type of games are people searching for every month. One can cater their concept to a specific market, such as people looking for science based games or math, or games for women, games you can play with friends, etc.

If your goal is to churn out artistically bereft AI slop games to try to maximize profit, maybe.  

Nobody making the Shovel Knight or Binding of Isaac or Super Mario Bros started with "Hmm, which *market segment of gamer* is the most exploitably profitable..."  followed by a bunch of slop prototypes trying to go viral. They set out to make a *genuinely good game* in their genre of choice.

It's wise to spend most of your time *in the pursuit of being excellent in your craft*, unless your goal is to be a slop shoveler for profit.

comments.author: Over-Clerk-5307
comments.body:
imo a lot of people are caught up on being a "real programmer," as if writing code makes you a good computer scientist or a good software engineer

  
the trick is that we no longer have to code, but we still have to articulate the same principles of logic, reasoning, robustness, edge case handling, blah blah blah. You don't get to skip all of the thinking involved in making a game; it's a different type of higher level thinking akin to being a manager (which most of us aren't nor have ever been).

the barrier to code is gone, but the skill of knowing what to ask for, how to test and articulate bugs (or undesired behavior that's logically correct but not quite "right"), having quality taste, and how to HAVE FUN MAKING GAMES is something AI cannot do for us.
